# 1 Maccabees Chapter 10 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 10 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/1MA_010_page_001.jpg

---

**1** In 152 BCE, Alexander Epiphanes — son of Antiochus — sailed in, took the port of Ptolemais, and was welcomed as king.

**2** Demetrius got the news and mobilized a massive army to fight him.

**3** But he also wrote to Jonathan — a friendly letter, designed to flatter and win him over.

**4** His reasoning was simple: "We need to make a deal with the Jews before Alexander does. If Alexander gets them first, they'll fight us.

**5** And Jonathan hasn't forgotten what we did to him and his family and his people."

**6** So Demetrius authorized Jonathan to raise and arm troops, named him a royal ally, and ordered the hostages in the Jerusalem citadel released to him.

**7** Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the royal letters in public — before all the people and the citadel garrison alike.

**8** When they heard that the king had given Jonathan the power to raise an army, the garrison was terrified.

**9** They handed over the hostages. Jonathan reunited them with their families.

**10** Jonathan moved back into Jerusalem and started rebuilding the city.

**11** He commissioned the construction of defensive walls around Jerusalem and Mount Zion, using dressed stone, and the work went ahead.

**12** The foreign garrisons in the Bacchides fortresses began to abandon their posts —

**13** every man packing up and going home.

**14** The only holdouts were at Beth-zur, where Jewish apostates had made their base, treating it as a safe haven from the new order.

**15** Meanwhile, Alexander had been hearing reports about Jonathan — Demetrius's promises, the battles Jonathan and his brothers had fought, everything they had endured.

**16** Alexander said: "There's no one else like him. Let's make him our friend right now."

**17** He wrote Jonathan a letter:

**18** "King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings.

**19** We have heard about you. You are a man of valor, and you deserve to be our friend.

**20** We therefore appoint you high priest of your nation this day. You shall bear the title Friend of the King." — He sent with the letter a purple robe and a gold crown. — "Align yourself with us, and let us maintain our friendship."

**21** That autumn — at the Feast of Tabernacles in 152 BCE — Jonathan put on the priestly vestments for the first time and set about raising and equipping an army.

**22** When Demetrius heard, he felt the sting of it and said:

**23** "What are we doing? Alexander beat us to the Jews — the very people we need for support.

**24** I'll write to them too. Compliments, honors, gifts — whatever it takes to bring them over to my side."

**25** His letter read: "King Demetrius to the Jewish nation, greetings.

**26** You have honored your commitments to us, stayed in our camp, and refused to side with our enemies. We have heard of this, and we are pleased.

**27** Keep it up, and we will pay you well for your loyalty.

**28** We are prepared to grant you sweeping exemptions and gifts.

**29** Effective immediately: I am releasing all Jews from tribute, from the salt tax, and from crown taxes.

**30** I am also canceling the collection of one-third of the grain and one-half of the fruit harvest — rights that normally belong to me. As of today, these levies are abolished forever. This applies to Judea and to the three districts I have added from Samaria and Galilee.

**31** Jerusalem and its surrounding territory shall be sacred and tax-exempt.

**32** I am surrendering my claim to the Jerusalem citadel and transferring it to the high priest, to garrison as he sees fit.

**33** Every Jewish captive anywhere in my kingdom, I set free without ransom, and all their tax obligations — including livestock taxes — are cancelled.

**34** Every feast day, every Sabbath, every new moon, every sacred calendar date — plus three days before and three days after each feast — shall be days of full legal immunity for all Jews throughout my kingdom.

**35** No one shall have the right to demand payment from them or harass them in any way.

**36** I will enroll thirty thousand Jews in my royal forces with full pay and benefits, equal to any other soldier; some shall be stationed in my major fortresses,

**37** and some shall hold positions of trust throughout the kingdom. Their officers and commanders shall be Jews, and they shall be governed by their own law, as I have decreed for Judea.

**38** The three Samaritan districts added to Judea shall be fully absorbed into Judea and answerable only to the high priest — no other authority.

**39** The revenues from Ptolemais and its region I donate to the Jerusalem temple for its operating expenses.

**40** I pledge fifteen thousand shekels of silver per year from the royal budget for the temple's needs.

**41** Any back payments that royal officials owe and have never paid — these shall now go to the temple treasury.

**42** Furthermore, the five thousand shekels taken annually from temple income in the past shall be restored — those funds belong to the priests.

**43** Anyone who takes sanctuary at the Jerusalem temple — whatever debts or charges they face — they shall be free, and all their property in my kingdom shall be immune from seizure.

**44** The renovation and maintenance of the sanctuary shall be funded from the royal treasury.

**45** The rebuilding and fortification of Jerusalem's walls, and the fortification of towns throughout Judea — all funded from the royal treasury."

**46** Jonathan and the people listened to all of this and paid it no mind. They couldn't trust Demetrius — they hadn't forgotten the tremendous suffering he had inflicted on Israel.

**47** Alexander had spoken first, and that mattered. Jonathan and his people threw in their lot with Alexander for good.

**48** Alexander pulled together a large army and took up position against Demetrius.

**49** The two kings clashed. Demetrius's army broke and fled; Alexander ran them down.

**50** The fighting lasted till sundown. When it was over, Demetrius was dead.

**51** Alexander then sent a diplomatic mission to Ptolemy VI of Egypt with this message:

**52** "Now that I have come home to my kingdom, reclaimed my throne, and defeated Demetrius —

**53** I engaged him in battle and crushed him, and now I sit on his throne —

**54** let us seal an alliance. Give me your daughter as my wife. I will be your son-in-law, and I will honor you and her with gifts befitting your stature."

**55** Ptolemy wrote back: "A happy day it is that you have come home and claimed the throne of your fathers.

**56** I will do what you ask. Come to Ptolemais and let us meet, and I will give you my daughter in marriage, as you have said."

**57** Ptolemy traveled from Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra and arrived at Ptolemais in 150 BCE.

**58** Alexander came to meet him. Ptolemy gave his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander in a magnificent royal wedding.

**59** Alexander wrote to Jonathan, summoning him to the celebration.

**60** Jonathan arrived at Ptolemais in state, presented both kings and their entourages with silver, gold, and lavish gifts, and found himself in high favor.

**61** Some troublemakers — Jewish renegades — had come to Ptolemais to lodge accusations against him. The king dismissed them without a hearing.

**62** The king ordered that Jonathan be stripped of his own clothing and dressed in royal purple, and this was done.

**63** The king seated Jonathan at his own side, then said to his officers: "Escort him through the center of the city and announce publicly that no one may bring any charge against him or trouble him in any matter whatsoever."

**64** When his accusers saw Jonathan clothed in purple and honored by royal proclamation, they fled in all directions.

**65** The king formally honored Jonathan, enrolled him among his principal friends, and appointed him general and provincial governor.

**66** Jonathan returned home to Jerusalem in peace and in good spirits.

**67** In 147 BCE, Demetrius II, son of Demetrius I, crossed from Crete and landed in his ancestral territory.

**68** Alexander was shaken when he heard the news and retreated to Antioch.

**69** Demetrius II appointed a commander named Apollonius as governor of Coele-Syria. Apollonius assembled a large force and established himself at Jamnia, then sent a taunting message to Jonathan:

**70** "You're the only one standing against us — and you've made a laughingstock of me. Why do you think you can play at power up in the hills?

**71** If you're confident in your troops, come down to the plain and let's settle this, because the cities are on my side.

**72** Ask around and find out who I am and who backs me. You'll learn that you cannot stand against us — your own ancestors were routed twice in their own land.

**73** In open country, against my cavalry and my numbers, you won't last — there's no stone, no cliff, no place to hide."

**74** That challenge got under Jonathan's skin. He personally selected ten thousand men and marched out of Jerusalem. Simon came along to back him up.

**75** He moved on Joppa first. The city shut its gates against him — Apollonius had a garrison there. He attacked anyway.

**76** The terrified citizens opened the gates. Jonathan had Joppa.

**77** Apollonius heard and moved — three thousand cavalry and a large infantry force, heading toward Azotus as though just passing through. In reality, he was drawing Jonathan into the plain, counting on his cavalry to win it there.

**78** Jonathan took the bait and pursued him to Azotus. They met in battle.

**79** But Apollonius had a surprise: he had quietly left one thousand cavalry hidden in the rear.

**80** Jonathan walked into the trap. His forces were surrounded and pelted with arrows for an entire day — dawn to dusk.

**81** His men held. Jonathan's orders were to stand firm, and they did, even as the enemy horses tired.

**82** At that moment Simon advanced his division and struck the phalanx. The cavalry had worn itself out; it broke and ran.

**83** The horsemen scattered across the plain, fled into Azotus, and took shelter in the temple of Dagon — their god.

**84** Jonathan burned Azotus and every town around it, plundering them all. The temple of Dagon, with everyone who had taken refuge in it, he burned to the ground.

**85** Counting those killed in the fighting and those burned in the temple, the dead numbered about eight thousand men.

**86** Jonathan moved on and encamped before Ashkelon. The city's population came out to greet him with full ceremony.

**87** Jonathan and his forces returned to Jerusalem loaded with plunder.

**88** When Alexander heard what had happened, he heaped more honors on Jonathan

**89** and sent him a golden clasp — the mark of royal kinship — and awarded him the city of Ekron and all its surrounding territory as his personal possession.
